facts.statement: A time series is a set of observations collected at successive points in time or over successive periods, at regular intervals. It is used in economic, budget, sales and profit forecasting. Forecast quality depends on the information in past data and its validity.

A time series has four types of variation. Secular trend is the smooth, general, long-term tendency to increase, decrease or stay constant (the Consumer Price Index rising over years). Cyclical fluctuation is movement above and below the trend over periods longer than a year, as in the business cycle, with irregular periods and amplitude. Seasonal variation is a regular pattern of change within a year (flu cases in winter, tourists at hill resorts in summer). Irregular variation is unpredictable, random change from events such as earthquakes, floods and wars. Real series usually contain several of these components.

Trend analysis describes the long-term direction. Reasons to study it: to describe historical patterns and judge past policies, to project the future (such as population and GDP growth), and to separate the trend so that seasonal and other components can be seen clearly. A trend a straight line can describe is linear; some trends are curvilinear (pollution rising, the life cycle of a product with a growth phase and then a decline). The linear trend is y-hat = a + bx with x the time variable.

To simplify the fitting of the trend line the time variable is coded so that its mean is zero. For an odd number of years code x = year - mean year (for 2012 to 2016: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2). For an even number of years the mean falls between two years, so the deviations (-2.5, -1.5, ...) are multiplied by 2 to give odd whole numbers (-5, -3, -1, 1, 3, 5). With coded time the slope is b = Sum xy / Sum x^2 and the intercept is a = y-bar. To forecast for a year, convert it to coded time first (for the courseware's ship data with mean year 2017.5, x = 2 (2024 - 2017.5) = 13). For its eight years of ships loaded (98, 105, 116, 119, 135, 156, 177, 208) the courseware finds Sum y = 1,114, Sum xy = 1,266, Sum x^2 = 168, b = 7.536 and a = 139.25, so the forecast for 2024 is 237.

A curvilinear trend may be fitted with a parabola, y-hat = a + bx + cx^2, using coded time. The constants satisfy Sum y = n a + c Sum x^2, Sum x^2 y = a Sum x^2 + c Sum x^4 and b = Sum xy / Sum x^2. For the courseware's five years of watch sales (13, 24, 39, 65, 106) with codes -2 to 2: Sum x^2 = 10, Sum x^4 = 34, Sum xy = 227, Sum x^2 y = 565 and Sum y = 247, giving b = 22.7, c = 5.07 and a = 39.3.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 92-93, Using Second Degree Trends and the watch example

facts.statement: Cyclical variation is isolated by the residual method: percent of trend = (y / y-hat) x 100 and relative cyclical residual = ((y - y-hat) / y-hat) x 100, where y is the actual and y-hat the trend value. Values above 100 per cent of trend (positive residuals) show actual above the trend. The technique can be used only to analyse past cyclical variation, not to predict future cyclical variation.

Seasonal variation is repetitive and predictable, and must be measured in short intervals such as days, weeks or quarters. Establishing the seasonal pattern allows prediction and allows its effect to be removed from the series (deseasonalisation). The ratio-to-moving-average method gives a seasonal index based on 100: if a resort rents 20,000 boats a year the average quarter is 5,000, and an index of 142 for the summer quarter gives an estimate of 5,000 x 142/100 = 7,100.

The ratio-to-moving-average method for quarterly data: (1) total each run of four quarters, sliding forward one quarter at a time; (2) divide each total by 4 for the four-quarter moving average; (3) centre it by averaging each pair of consecutive moving averages (needed for an even number of periods, not for an odd number such as seven days); (4) express each actual value as a percentage of its centred moving average, 100 x actual / average; (5) for each quarter take the modified mean of its percentages, discarding the highest and lowest values to remove extreme cyclical and irregular effects; (6) because the four indices should total 400, multiply each modified mean by the adjusting constant 400 / (sum of the modified means). In the courseware example the modified means 91.25, 107.70, 113.25 and 91.90 total 404.10 and the constant is 0.9899.

Deseasonalised value = actual value / (seasonal index / 100); it shows only the trend, cyclical and irregular components. A trend can be fitted to the deseasonalised data and used for prediction; the deseasonalised forecast is then multiplied by the seasonal index / 100 to get the forecast for the season (2,121 x 91.0/100 = 1,930 rooms in the courseware example).
facts.locator: Printed p. 98, Use of Seasonal Index

facts.statement: Irregular variation is what remains after removing trend, cyclical and seasonal variation: unpredictable factors acting over very short intervals and following random patterns (an unusually cold winter raising electricity use, wars raising air and train travel). Their causes may not be identifiable, but over time such random variations tend to correct themselves. A series with all four components (trend, seasonal, cyclical, irregular) is handled by deseasonalising it, fitting the trend line to the deseasonalised data and then computing the per cent of trend.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 99-101, sections 5.6 and the four-component example

facts.statement: Time-series forecasting predicts future values from past data on the assumption that future trends will resemble historical ones. Three basic models are the autoregressive model (AR: a linear combination of past values of the variable, a regression of the variable on itself), the moving-average model (MA: the error term modelled as a linear combination of current and past error terms) and the ARMA model (a combination of the two, considering the impact of previous lags and the residuals).

payload.title: The four components of a time series
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **time series** is a set of readings taken at regular intervals: monthly deposits, quarterly profit, yearly new accounts. Four forces shape it:

| Component | What it is | Banking example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Secular trend** | Smooth long-term drift, up or down | Steady growth of digital transactions over a decade |
| **Cyclical** | Swings above and below the trend over several years, uneven in length | Credit growth rising and slumping with the business cycle |
| **Seasonal** | Regular pattern within a year | Cash demand peaking around festivals each year |
| **Irregular** | Random, unpredictable shocks | Flood closing branches in a district for a week |

Real data mix all four. Time series analysis tries to pull them apart.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A quick test: if the pattern repeats on a calendar rhythm (every year, every quarter), it is seasonal. If it swings over several years with no fixed length, it is cyclical.

self_check.prompt_text: Quarterly cash withdrawals jump every December. Which component is that, and what distinguishes it from a cyclical swing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal variation: it repeats on a fixed calendar rhythm within the year, while cyclical swings last longer than a year and vary in length.

payload.title: Why study the trend
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Treat any trend projection as conditional: it assumes the future resembles the past. A sudden break, such as a war or a regulatory change, can invalidate it.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three reasons for studying a trend.
self_check.expected_takeaway: To describe historical patterns, to project the future, and to separate the trend from other components.

payload.title: Linear trend with coded time
payload.core_explanation_md:
Fit the straight line y-hat = a + bx exactly as in regression, but use time as the independent variable, and **code** time so the arithmetic is easy.

- **Odd number of years**: let x be the year minus the middle year (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...).
- **Even number of years**: the middle falls between two years, so subtract the mean and **double** the result to get whole odd numbers (..., -3, -1, 1, 3, ...).

Because the codes add to zero, the formulas shrink: **a is simply the mean of y** and **b = Sum xy / Sum x squared**.

To forecast, first convert the future year to the same code: x = 2 x (year minus mean year) for an even series.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The most common slip is plugging the calendar year (2026) into the equation instead of its coded value. Always code the target year with the same rule you used for the data.

self_check.expected_takeaway: b = 258/70 = 3.69; because the codes step by 2 per year, the trend rises 3.69 per half-year, that is about 7.37 per year.

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A parabola fits the data in hand very well; its forecasts further out can be wild, because the squared term grows quickly. Check that the curve is sensible before relying on it.

payload.title: Cyclical variation by the residual method
payload.core_explanation_md:
Once the trend is fitted, what is left over is cycle plus irregular noise. To see the cycle, compare each actual value with its trend value:

- **Per cent of trend** = actual / trend x 100. Above 100 means above trend.
- **Relative cyclical residual** = (actual - trend) / trend x 100. Positive means above trend, negative below.

Plot these over time. Stretches above 100 and then below 100 reveal the cycle.

The method describes the **past** cycle. It cannot forecast the next one, because cycles do not repeat at fixed intervals.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The relative residual is just per cent of trend minus 100. Using either is fine; check which one a question asks for.

variables.name: Trend value for the same period

assumptions: The trend has already been fitted and removed from the comparison.
common_errors: Dividing by the actual value instead of the trend value.
Reporting per cent of trend where the residual is asked (a difference of 100).
Using the result to forecast future cycles.

self_check.prompt_text: Actual 66, trend 60. What are the per cent of trend and the relative cyclical residual?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 66/60 x 100 = 110 per cent of trend; residual = (66 - 60)/60 x 100 = 10 per cent.

payload.title: Seasonal index by ratio to moving average: the six steps
payload.core_explanation_md:
A seasonal index says how a quarter usually compares with an average quarter, with 100 as average. To build it from quarterly data:

1. **Moving total** of four quarters, sliding one quarter at a time.
2. **Moving average**: divide by 4.
3. **Centre** it: average each pair of consecutive moving averages, so the result lines up with an actual quarter. (Skip this for an odd period like 7 days.)
4. **Ratio**: 100 x actual / centred average, for every quarter that has one.
5. **Modified mean** of each quarter's ratios, dropping the highest and lowest to cut out extreme cyclical and irregular effects.
6. **Adjust** so the four indices total 400: multiply each by 400 divided by the sum of the modified means.

The moving average smooths out seasons and random bumps, leaving trend plus cycle, so the ratio isolates season plus irregular.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Why centre? A four-quarter average naturally falls between two quarters. Averaging two neighbours moves it onto a quarter so you can divide that quarter's actual by it.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are modified means rescaled so the indices total 400?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal indices are based on 100 per quarter, so across four quarters they must average 100 and total 400; the modified means may not, so they are scaled by 400 divided by their sum.

payload.title: Using a seasonal index: deseasonalise, then forecast
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two uses, one inverse of the other:

- **Deseasonalise** (remove the season): actual / (index / 100). This shows trend, cycle and irregular movement only, so you can compare quarters fairly. A quarter that looks weak may simply be a seasonally weak quarter.
- **Forecast with the season** (put it back): estimate the trend on deseasonalised data, then multiply the deseasonalised forecast by index / 100.

Example: a deseasonalised forecast of 2,000 for a quarter whose index is 90 becomes 2,000 x 90/100 = 1,800.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Always check the direction. Dividing by the index removes the season; multiplying by it restores the season.

self_check.prompt_text: A quarter's actual cash demand is 1,134 and its seasonal index is 126. What is the deseasonalised value?

payload.title: Irregular variation, the combined model and forecasting models
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Irregular variation** is what is left after trend, cycle and season are taken out: random shocks such as a flood or an unusually cold winter. We cannot predict it, but over time it tends to even out.

To handle all four components in one series:

1. deseasonalise the data with the seasonal index;
2. fit the trend line to the deseasonalised data;
3. compute per cent of trend to see what remains (cycle plus irregular).

For forecasting from a series' own history there are three families of models:

| Model | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Autoregressive (AR) | Predict from a combination of the variable's own past values |
| Moving average (MA) | Model the error as a combination of present and past errors |
| ARMA | Both together |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: All time-series forecasting assumes the future will resemble the past. When structure changes (a new regulation, a crisis), the forecast can fail.

self_check.prompt_text: In what order do you treat the components of a quarterly series with all four present?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deseasonalise with the seasonal index, fit the trend to the deseasonalised data, then use per cent of trend to look at cycle and irregular variation.

items.title: The four components of a time series
items.core_explanation_md:
A **time series** is a set of readings taken at regular intervals: monthly deposits, quarterly profit, yearly new accounts. Four forces shape it:

| Component | What it is | Banking example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Secular trend** | Smooth long-term drift, up or down | Steady growth of digital transactions over a decade |
| **Cyclical** | Swings above and below the trend over several years, uneven in length | Credit growth rising and slumping with the business cycle |
| **Seasonal** | Regular pattern within a year | Cash demand peaking around festivals each year |
| **Irregular** | Random, unpredictable shocks | Flood closing branches in a district for a week |

Real data mix all four. Time series analysis tries to pull them apart.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A quick test: if the pattern repeats on a calendar rhythm (every year, every quarter), it is seasonal. If it swings over several years with no fixed length, it is cyclical.

self_check.prompt_text: Quarterly cash withdrawals jump every December. Which component is that, and what distinguishes it from a cyclical swing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal variation: it repeats on a fixed calendar rhythm within the year, while cyclical swings last longer than a year and vary in length.

items.title: Linear trend with coded time
items.core_explanation_md:
Fit the straight line y-hat = a + bx exactly as in regression, but use time as the independent variable, and **code** time so the arithmetic is easy.

- **Odd number of years**: let x be the year minus the middle year (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...).
- **Even number of years**: the middle falls between two years, so subtract the mean and **double** the result to get whole odd numbers (..., -3, -1, 1, 3, ...).

Because the codes add to zero, the formulas shrink: **a is simply the mean of y** and **b = Sum xy / Sum x squared**.

To forecast, first convert the future year to the same code: x = 2 x (year minus mean year) for an even series.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The most common slip is plugging the calendar year (2026) into the equation instead of its coded value. Always code the target year with the same rule you used for the data.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \hat{y} = a + bx,\quad a = \bar{y},\quad b = \frac{\sum xy}{\sum x^2}\ \ (\text{coded } x,\ \textstyle\sum x = 0)

variables.name: Coded time (zero mean)
variables.unit: coded units: years, or half-years when doubled

variables.name: Mean of y: value of the trend at x = 0
Trend change per coded unit
variables.unit: units of the series per coded unit

assumptions: The trend is a straight line.
Coding rule for the forecast year matches the rule used for the data.
common_errors: Forecasting with the calendar year instead of the coded value.
Forgetting that the doubled code changes the meaning of b (change per half-year).
Using a different mean year for the forecast than for the data.

self_check.prompt_text: Six years are coded -5, -3, -1, 1, 3, 5. If Sum xy = 258 and Sum x squared = 70, what is b, and what does b mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: b = 258/70 = 3.69; because the codes step by 2 per year, the trend rises 3.69 per half-year, that is about 7.37 per year.

items.title: Cyclical variation by the residual method
items.core_explanation_md:
Once the trend is fitted, what is left over is cycle plus irregular noise. To see the cycle, compare each actual value with its trend value:

- **Per cent of trend** = actual / trend x 100. Above 100 means above trend.
- **Relative cyclical residual** = (actual - trend) / trend x 100. Positive means above trend, negative below.

Plot these over time. Stretches above 100 and then below 100 reveal the cycle.

The method describes the **past** cycle. It cannot forecast the next one, because cycles do not repeat at fixed intervals.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relative residual is just per cent of trend minus 100. Using either is fine; check which one a question asks for.

variables.name: Trend value for the same period

assumptions: The trend has already been fitted and removed from the comparison.
common_errors: Dividing by the actual value instead of the trend value.
Reporting per cent of trend where the residual is asked (a difference of 100).
Using the result to forecast future cycles.

self_check.prompt_text: Actual 66, trend 60. What are the per cent of trend and the relative cyclical residual?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 66/60 x 100 = 110 per cent of trend; residual = (66 - 60)/60 x 100 = 10 per cent.

items.title: Seasonal index by ratio to moving average: the six steps
items.core_explanation_md:
A seasonal index says how a quarter usually compares with an average quarter, with 100 as average. To build it from quarterly data:

1. **Moving total** of four quarters, sliding one quarter at a time.
2. **Moving average**: divide by 4.
3. **Centre** it: average each pair of consecutive moving averages, so the result lines up with an actual quarter. (Skip this for an odd period like 7 days.)
4. **Ratio**: 100 x actual / centred average, for every quarter that has one.
5. **Modified mean** of each quarter's ratios, dropping the highest and lowest to cut out extreme cyclical and irregular effects.
6. **Adjust** so the four indices total 400: multiply each by 400 divided by the sum of the modified means.

The moving average smooths out seasons and random bumps, leaving trend plus cycle, so the ratio isolates season plus irregular.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why centre? A four-quarter average naturally falls between two quarters. Averaging two neighbours moves it onto a quarter so you can divide that quarter's actual by it.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are modified means rescaled so the indices total 400?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal indices are based on 100 per quarter, so across four quarters they must average 100 and total 400; the modified means may not, so they are scaled by 400 divided by their sum.

items.title: Using a seasonal index: deseasonalise, then forecast
items.core_explanation_md:
Two uses, one inverse of the other:

- **Deseasonalise** (remove the season): actual / (index / 100). This shows trend, cycle and irregular movement only, so you can compare quarters fairly. A quarter that looks weak may simply be a seasonally weak quarter.
- **Forecast with the season** (put it back): estimate the trend on deseasonalised data, then multiply the deseasonalised forecast by index / 100.

Example: a deseasonalised forecast of 2,000 for a quarter whose index is 90 becomes 2,000 x 90/100 = 1,800.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Always check the direction. Dividing by the index removes the season; multiplying by it restores the season.

items.title: Irregular variation, the combined model and forecasting models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Irregular variation** is what is left after trend, cycle and season are taken out: random shocks such as a flood or an unusually cold winter. We cannot predict it, but over time it tends to even out.

To handle all four components in one series:

1. deseasonalise the data with the seasonal index;
2. fit the trend line to the deseasonalised data;
3. compute per cent of trend to see what remains (cycle plus irregular).

For forecasting from a series' own history there are three families of models:

| Model | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Autoregressive (AR) | Predict from a combination of the variable's own past values |
| Moving average (MA) | Model the error as a combination of present and past errors |
| ARMA | Both together |
items.expanded_explanation_md: All time-series forecasting assumes the future will resemble the past. When structure changes (a new regulation, a crisis), the forecast can fail.

self_check.prompt_text: In what order do you treat the components of a quarterly series with all four present?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deseasonalise with the seasonal index, fit the trend to the deseasonalised data, then use per cent of trend to look at cycle and irregular variation.

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 1 decimal place.

items.correct_explanation_md: Relative cyclical residual = (55 - 50) / 50 x 100 = 10.0.
